## Function assignment and case

*She was handing him some broccoli.*

| Selected pronoun | Assigned function | Form |
|---|---|---|
| Feminine | Nominative / subject | **she** |
| Masculine | Dative / recipient object | **him** |

If the functions are exchanged: *He was handing her some broccoli.*

::: {.prompt}
Why do we get *he* and *her*, rather than *him* and *she*?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, I and III.A
:::

::: {.notes}
Start with the forms. Selecting a pronoun does not by itself determine
whether it will be she or her, he or him. Its grammatical function matters.
In the exchange, the masculine pronoun receives nominative and comes out as
he. The feminine pronoun receives dative and comes out as her.

The chapter's observed error they must be too tight for you becoming you
must be too tight for them has the same property. The pronoun takes the case
appropriate to its erroneous function. Verbs in phrase exchanges also tend
to agree with the subject actually produced. These are reasons to locate the
exchange before the final case and agreement forms are fixed.

The authors use case labels for functional assignments. English him does not
have a special dative form distinct from its other object uses. Dative here
names the function assigned in their analysis.

If needed, distinguish function from event role and position. The bone is the
theme in both a dog carried the bone and the bone was carried by a dog, but
its function differs. Him is an object even in him I can't stand. In the
chapter's proposal, functions are assigned once and then maintained during
assembly.
:::

## Assigning nominative first

> "... at least in English, there is a preference for combinations of elements
> that permit the nominative function to be assigned first."

*She seems to be feeding the dog.*

::: {.prompt}
What must the speaker have planned before assigning nominative to *she*?
Which verb determines her role in the event: *seems* or *feeding*?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, III.B.2, p. 966; classroom example
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the quotation, then give students a minute with the sentence. Ask them
to propose a planning order: which lemmas and grammatical relations would
need to be available before the speaker begins with she?

She is the subject of seems, but her agent role comes from feeding. Seems
does not describe a separate action that she performs. How does the planner
connect that participant to the nominative function of the main clause?

Ask whether selecting seems is enough, or whether the speaker also needs
information about feeding and its agent. How much of the lower clause must
be prepared? Would the dog need to be selected already? Let students compare
possible procedures before offering an answer.

The quotation proposes a preference for assigning nominative before other
functions. It does not specify that the nominative expression must be the
first lemma selected, or that its form is ready before either verb. The
preceding clause explicitly allows functions to be assigned in other orders
or simultaneously. This example asks what advance preparation the preference
requires when the subject's event role comes from a later verb.

The choice of verb constrains function assignment: compare many people fear
snakes with snakes frighten many people. Conceptual accessibility also matters.
Asking about the boy in a chasing scene can favor he was being chased by a girl.
The participant made prominent in discourse tends to become the subject.
:::

## Function words and affixes

For a definite, plural noun phrase: *the goats*.

| | Garrett | Lapointe and Dell |
|---|---|---|
| Article *the* | Already in the frame | Inserted into a definite determiner slot |
| Plural *-s* | Already in the frame | Already in the frame |
| Stem *goat* | Supplied separately | Supplied separately |

In Lapointe's aphasia data, function words tended to be **omitted**;
affixes tended to be **replaced**.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.A and V.B; example adapted from their definite plural NP
:::

::: {.notes}
What has to be supplied to produce the goats? We need the stem, definite
article, and plural marking. The two accounts disagree about which of these
are already specified in the frame.

For Garrett, the closed class elements help constitute the grammatical frame.
A definite plural noun phrase includes the article and plural suffix, with a
slot for the stem. Lapointe and Dell leave the affix in the frame but insert
the article into a slot specified as definite. They assume one filler for a
designated function-word slot, without competition among candidates.

The omission-versus-replacement pattern in English and Italian aphasic speech
motivated that distinction: affixes appeared more tightly tied to the frame.
Ask what an omitted article versus a replaced number affix would sound like
in the goats. This is an illustration of the distinction, not a quotation
of an individual patient's response.

Closed class elements also participate less often in spontaneous errors than
content words. Frequency is a competing explanation, because function words
are extremely frequent. Garrett cited class differences after frequency was
controlled and disproportionate loss of function words in some aphasic speech.

Bock found equally strong structural priming with the same or different
function words. That challenges an account equating the frame entirely with
those words. The repeated structure carries information beyond its particular
articles or prepositions.

At phonological encoding, Lapointe and Dell give function and content words
the same operations. Dell's elicited sound-error results supported similar
susceptibility when other factors were controlled.
:::

## Inflectional stranding

Intended: *You **ended** up **ordering** some fish dish.*

Produced: *You **ordered** up **ending** some fish dish.*

| | First verb | Second verb |
|---|---|---|
| Intended | **end** + ed | **order** + ing |
| Produced | **order** + ed | **end** + ing |

The stems exchange; the inflections stay. Both frame accounts predict this.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; Garrett, cited as in press
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the produced sentence aloud. Ask students to identify the pieces that
moved before walking through the table. A swap of the whole words would have
moved the inflections too.

Both Garrett's model and the mixed model explain this as a lexical error
with an intact frame. The appropriate inflectional slots remain available,
but the wrong stems fill them. This tells us why stranding is evidence for
separate stem and affix assembly without choosing between the two accounts.

Stemberger found stranding in 88.9 percent of the errors where it was possible
in his corpus. The denominator is eligible errors, not all speech errors.

The authors use errors along morphological boundaries to challenge accounts
that give regular inflected forms no explicit stem-and-affix organization.
Those accounts would still have to explain why stems exchange while inflections
remain appropriate to their positions.

The next question is how those positions acquired their grammatical features.
Where does a plural specification come from, and how does it lead to a form?
:::

## Plural number and its realization

| Selected noun | SINGULAR | PLURAL |
|---|---|---|
| *goat* | goat | goat + **s** |
| *sheep* | sheep | sheep |

**PLURAL** is a grammatical feature. Its realization depends on the noun.

::: {.prompt}
*Two sheep are outside.* Which word shows number agreement, even though
*sheep* has no plural suffix?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; classroom sentence
:::

::: {.notes}
Work across each row. Goat has a visible difference between singular and
plural; sheep does not. A speaker still needs a plural specification for
plural sheep. The absence of a suffix does not remove grammatical number.

The chapter describes this through the selected lemma's requirements. A plural
goat lemma calls for a noun phrase with an affix on the head noun. A plural
sheep lemma calls for no affix. This extends indirect election: a selected
lemma requires particular grammatical material, as listen requires to.

In two sheep are outside, two tells us the quantity, and are shows plural
agreement. Compare one sheep is outside. The noun's pronunciation stays the
same while the verb changes. Give students a moment to explain why an account
that simply looks for a plural suffix on the noun would fail here.

For the chapter's architecture, keep the grammatical specification at the
lemma level distinct from its eventual form. In a regular plural, positional
processing provides the stem-and-affix arrangement, and phonological encoding
supplies its pronunciation.
:::

## How does the verb get its number?

*The **key** to the cabinets **is** missing.*

*The **keys** to the cabinet **are** missing.*

| In the first sentence | What gets specified |
|---|---|
| Subject head | *key*: SINGULAR |
| Agreement | The finite verb receives the subject's number |
| Realization | Present-tense *be*, third-person singular: **is** |

Attraction error: *The key to the cabinets **are** missing.*

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; classroom examples
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask which noun controls the verb in each sentence. The subject head does:
key goes with is, keys with are. The nearest noun gives the wrong answer in
both examples. An agreeing verb needs access to the structural relation.

Walk through the table for the first sentence. Functional processing links
the noun lemma key to the subject function, with singular number. The finite
verb needs the same number. Bock and Levelt favor the proposal that it inherits
number from the subject. Present tense, third person, and singular together
require is here. Grammatical features must be available before the final
inflected form can be produced.

This is agreement: the verb's number is dependent on the subject's number.
It is different from choosing plural because the message contains several
objects. The first sentence describes several cabinets but still requires is.

Now read the error. Cabinets has influenced agreement even though it is not
the head of the subject. The output has a real plural verb form in the wrong
dependency. Attraction is therefore useful evidence about the features used
to produce inflection.

For a regular verb, compare the key fits and the keys fit. The noun suffix
marks plural in keys; the verb suffix marks third-person singular in fits.
The same written s does different grammatical work. Agreement requires matching
features, not copying a suffix from the noun onto the verb.
:::

## Which property causes attraction?

*The picture of the ___ **is** on the wall.*

| Local noun | Grammatical number | Ends in /s/ or /z/? |
|---|---|---|
| cabinet | Singular | No |
| cabinets | Plural | Yes |
| children | Plural | No |
| rose | Singular | Yes |

In the studies reviewed, **grammatical plurality** reliably caused attraction,
including when the plural was irregular.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, V.C; Bock & Miller 1991; Bock & Eberhard 1993; classroom items
:::

::: {.notes}
The previous slide identified the wrong source of agreement. This slide asks
which property of that noun causes interference. The examples illustrate the
comparisons; they are not the original study's item set.

Cabinets bundles together several objects, grammatical plural number, and a
plural-sounding ending. Children is grammatically plural without a final s
or z. Rose is singular despite its final z. Cabinet supplies a singular
comparison without that ending.

Before discussing the finding, ask which nouns a sound-based account would
predict to interfere. It should group cabinets with rose. An account based
on grammatical number groups cabinets with children. The studies reviewed
found reliable effects of grammatical plurality, rather than plural-like
pronunciation or regularity of plural marking.

They also tested conceptual multiplicity. That did not reliably produce
attraction in these studies. This matters because the authors use attraction
to argue that lemmas supply number features to agreement. It is their inference
from the experiments reviewed here, not a claim that meaning never affects
agreement.

For an actual experiment, use several nouns per condition and control lexical
properties. These four different nouns alone would not establish an effect
of number or sound. Count plural finite verbs out of the completions in which
agreement can be scored.
:::

## Agreement across a clause boundary

**Phrase:** *The claim [about the newborn babies] ...*

**Clause:** *The claim [that wolves had raised the babies] ...*

In both, singular *claim* requires **was**. Plural *babies* can attract **were**.

::: {.fragment}
Errors were more likely after phrase modifiers. Putting *babies* in an
embedded clause reduced its interference with main-clause agreement.
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, III.C; Bock & Cutting 1992
:::

::: {.notes}
Claim is the singular head of the subject. Babies is plural and can attract
plural agreement: the claim about the newborn babies were rejected.

Bock and Cutting asked speakers to complete subject phrases. The critical
fragments ended in a plural noun, either inside a phrase or inside an embedded
clause. The study controlled syllable length; the examples here are the
chapter's illustrations.

Ask for predictions before showing the result. If the extra clause adds a
disruptive processing load, it could cause more errors. If verbs organize
separate planning units, babies could interfere less when it belongs to raised.

Across three experiments, errors were more frequent after phrase modifiers.
The authors take this as evidence for organization around verbs and their
arguments. The embedded clause reduced interference with the main clause's
agreement. It did not eliminate it.
:::

## Design an agreement experiment {.smaller}

| Modifier | Singular local noun | Plural local noun |
|---|---|---|
| Phrase | The claim about the newborn baby ... | The claim about the newborn babies ... |
| Clause | The claim that wolves had raised the baby ... | The claim that wolves had raised the babies ... |

Groups of three, ten minutes:

1. Write one new item in all four versions.
2. Specify how you will elicit and score agreement.
3. Predict where speakers will produce a plural verb in error.
4. Identify one confound and address it.

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, III.C; class exercise based on Bock & Cutting 1992
:::

::: {.notes}
Allow ten minutes for groups of three, then hear two reports. Each group
writes a new item in all four conditions and explains what they would count.
These four conditions are a class design exercise based on the chapter.

The singular local noun provides a baseline within each modifier type.
Protection predicts a larger plural-minus-singular increase in errors for
phrase modifiers than for clause modifiers.

Ask how groups will elicit number-marked finite verbs. They need to decide how
to score self-corrections and completions that change the subject or contain
no audible number contrast. Recordings let them count errors speakers may
not notice.

Each participant should see one version of each item. Rotate the versions
across lists, use multiple items and fillers, and vary the order. Match length
and plausibility. The original study controlled syllable length.

Wolves is another plural noun in the clause conditions. Groups could replace
it with the doctor and consider the effects on length and meaning. During
reports, ask for the predicted pattern and one change to the materials.
:::

## Change the subject

*She **was** hand**ing** him some broccoli.*

| Grammatical information | Realization in this sentence |
|---|---|
| Subject and object functions | **she**, **him** |
| Past progressive | **was** + hand**ing** |
| Singular subject agreement | **was** |

::: {.prompt}
Replace *she* with *they*. Which forms change? Which stay?
Where does the information for each change come from?
:::

::: footer
Bock & Levelt 1994, VI, Fig. 6; classroom comparison
:::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute to write the changed sentence and explain it.
The result is they were handing him some broccoli. They is the subject form
of the plural pronoun. Were replaces was because the subject's number has
changed. Handing stays progressive; him stays an object. The past tense and
the event's aspect have stayed the same.

The table makes a further point: was expresses more than one grammatical
specification. Features need not have separate, visibly segmentable affixes.
That is also why the chapter groups auxiliaries with affixes when discussing
how grammatical information is realized.

Ask what would change if the speaker intended a present ongoing event instead.
They are handing him some broccoli changes tense while preserving plural
agreement and progressive aspect. Use this to distinguish information about
the event from information required by a grammatical dependency.

In the chapter's architecture, functional processing provides lemmas,
functions, and feature dependencies. Positional processing assembles ordered
phrase structure and inflectional slots. Phonological encoding supplies forms.
These processes can work incrementally on parts of the utterance.

Constituent assembly provides hierarchy as well as order. The chapter contrasts
Yngve's top-down, left-to-right generator with de Smedt's incremental assembly
of compatible fragments. The agreement examples depend on that hierarchy:
the subject head and the finite verb must remain linked across intervening
material.

The chapter ends by arguing for explicit models tested against controlled
production data. Stranding and attraction constrain how a model connects
grammatical specifications to the forms speakers produce.
:::
